content: Recall bias, also known as reporting bias in psychology, is a systematic error that arises when a survey respondent's answer to a question is influenced not only by the correct or factual answer but also by the respondent's memory. This type of bias can distort the results of a survey. For instance, imagine a survey conducted in 2005 asking participants whether they believed O.J. Simpson had killed his wife, a decade after the criminal trial. Respondents who believed Simpson was innocent might be more likely to have forgotten details of the case and, as a result, might state that they have no opinion. On the other hand, those who believed he was guilty might retain stronger memories of the case and express their opinion more readily. If this pattern occurs, the survey could inaccurately reflect a higher proportion of people believing Simpson was guilty than is actually the case. A related but distinct form of recall bias occurs when a survey respondent deliberately provides an inaccurate answer about their personal history, leading to response bias. For example, consider a researcher conducting a survey among women in two different groups, Group A and Group B, asking whether they have had an abortion. If the survey results show differences between the two groups, it could be due to a genuine difference in abortion rates between the groups. However, it could also be that women in one group who have had abortions are less likely to admit to it. If the latter is true, this would skew the survey results. It is also possible that both factors are at play: women in one group may indeed have lower abortion rates, and those who have had abortions may also be less likely to disclose it. Either way, the survey statistics would be affected. In experimental sciences, the term reporting bias refers to the tendency to underreport unexpected or undesirable experimental results, often attributing such results to experimental error. Conversely, researchers may be more inclined to trust and report results that align with their expectations or are deemed desirable, even though these results may be equally subject to experimental errors. Over time, this type of bias can create a self-reinforcing cycle. For example, multiple researchers may independently discover and then discard unexpected results, assuming they are errors. Later researchers, observing that prior studies reported only expected results, may feel justified in dismissing their own unexpected findings as errors as well. This cumulative effect means that each instance of reporting bias increases the likelihood of future occurrences, perpetuating a distorted scientific record.
